explanation: After browser Back, a search box can retain text that is not the query applied to the restored page. That text may even have been submitted at a later point in history; in the reviewed cases the address and results correctly returned to the earlier search. This pattern matches a report that treats the box text alone as proof that the active query or results are wrong. Verify the restored submitted query and results separately; a later action silently applying the retained text or returning incorrect results is outside this rejection.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Sign in as eval and open the global Pull Requests dashboard at /pulls with an empty search field and visible unfiltered results. Type Update README.md into the search field and submit it. Confirm that the URL contains q=Update+README.md and the displayed results match the submitted search. Use browser Back. Observe the unfiltered /pulls URL and results while the field retains the draft typed before submission. For controls, use Forward to restore the applied search; then Back followed by Sort > Oldest. Confirm that sorting does not apply the retained search draft. The rejected report expected: After returning to the prior /pulls dashboard state, the search field is empty and the unfiltered list is shown. It claimed this outcome: After submitting “Update README.md” and using browser Back, the URL returned to /pulls and the unfiltered list returned, but the search field still displayed “Update README.md.” This remained visible after waiting six seconds. Review concluded: User rejected this as an inconsequential search-field display mismatch. Browser Back restores the draft that existed before explicit submission; the URL and results correctly restore the unfiltered list. Live controls confirmed that Forward restores the applied search, a matching search returns the correct PR, and sorting does not silently reapply the draft. Do not classify this reported draft retention alone as a product bug.

explanation: A test must actually activate the control whose behavior it claims to measure. This pattern matches reports where the input reached a neighboring element or popup, a drag never reached the required threshold, the editor was in the wrong mode, or a simulated key combination differed from the real shortcut. A click timeout or text appearing elsewhere therefore does not establish failure of the intended link, input or command. Confirm the event target, focus and complete gesture, then repeat the same intended action correctly before alleging its failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Sign in as eval on the pinned fixture and use a desktop viewport of1280×900. Create a disposable repository with README.md. Through the UI, create an editable branch and rename README.md to review notes.md without changing content. Create a PR and confirm Files Changed shows one file, zero additions and zero deletions. Open the far-right file-header ellipsis beside Viewed. Pointer-click View File and confirm the renamed file renders at the PR head commit. Return/reload/reopen and repeat; also verify Edit File opens its editor. Create another PR adding merged notes.md, merge it through the UI, and open Files Changed. Open the same file-header menu and pointer-click View File; confirm the added file renders. Reload/reopen and repeat. The rejected report expected: Visible View File and Edit File menu links should open the corresponding file or editor through normal pointer activation. It claimed this outcome: On an open rename-only PR with review notes.md and zero changed content lines, pointer View File twice and Edit File twice opened the correct rendered destinations; keyboard View also worked. On a merged added-file PR, pointer View File worked twice, including after reload and reopening the menu. Review concluded: Explicit user rejection after watching the exact-condition Mo recheck. Both named setups were recreated, actual pointer clicks reached the correct rendered destinations, and reload/reopen retries worked. The original tool timeout/intercepted-click reports did not establish an independently visible product failure.

explanation: A filter need not offer a separate option whose result would be identical to All. In the reviewed organization issue lists, a team with access to every repository is omitted from a filter whose purpose is choosing the team's repository set; that filter is also not a filter for who authored the items. This pattern matches a report that assumes the omitted team is missing functionality without checking what the filter narrows. An eligible narrower team absent, or an advertised author filter returning wrong results, is a separate claim.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Sign in as eval, an administrator, and create a disposable organization with two repositories. Create one open pull request in each repository. Create a team with All repositories access and Pull Requests Read. Join the team as eval and confirm its saved All repositories setting. Open the organization Pull Requests dashboard and its Teams menu, labelled Filter by team repositories. Observe All and the omission of the all-repositories team. For a control, create a second team with Specific repositories access and Pull Requests Read. Add only one of two organization repositories, each containing an open PR, and join as eval. Open the organization PR dashboard again. Confirm the specific-repository team appears; selecting it retains the assigned-repository PR and excludes the other repository’s PR. Returning to All restores both. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that an existing team with repository access must appear in the team filter, including when it is configured for All repositories. It claimed this outcome: The recorded team exists, includes eval as a member and has All repositories access, but the organization PR dashboard’s team-repository menu offers only All. Review concluded: User-approved rejection after source review and a live specific-repository control. The template explicitly omits teams with IncludesAllRepositories=true; this filter scopes repositories, not team-member authorship. The recorded All repositories team matches that excluded case. A limited team appears and filters its assigned repository’s PR correctly.

explanation: A short badge, selection count or secondary label often summarizes only part of an item's configuration. In the reviewed cases, a discount-type badge did not promise to show its amount, a selection count did not display both numeric bounds, or a shortened secondary label did not replace the full identity shown elsewhere. This pattern matches an inference of lost or wrong data from that abbreviated text while the full configuration and actual operation remain correct. Verify the detailed value or selected object before deciding that the summary proves corruption.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: From a fork, push a branch whose name is longer than 10 characters, such as forks-draft/path. Open New Pull Request comparing the base repository's main with that fork branch. Compare the branch shown in the 'pull from' selector with the name in the commits header on the right. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the comparison commit header shows the full head branch name. It claimed this outcome: With head branch alex:forks-draft/path, the selectors show the full name but the commit-list header reads main … forks-draf. Any branch name longer than 10 characters is shortened the same way, slash or not. Review concluded: User-rejected after reviewing the Mo reproduction and a screenshot. The full branch name stays visible in the branch selectors directly above, so the shortened label in the commit-list header is not treated as a product bug for this eval.

explanation: A markup editor turns typed symbols into formatting, so the exact saved characters determine what should appear. This pattern matches a report of broken Markdown rendering when the editor source actually lacks the claimed emphasis markers, already contains an automatically inserted task prefix, or lacks a separator required by the syntax. Compare the saved source with the output instead of assuming the intended keystrokes were all retained. Recreating a similar example later does not prove the historical input was identical.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: On a fresh pull request, enter the exact body - [ ] Confirm captain followed by a newline and - [x] Document verification, ensuring the editor contains exactly those two lines. Preview, save and reload; confirm Document verification is checked with no literal [x]. Separately, type the first unchecked item, press Enter, then type a complete - [x] Document verification marker after the automatically inserted prefix. Inspect the actual body: its second line is - [ ] - [x] Document verification. Preview renders that different input as an unchecked task with literal text. The rejected report expected: A valid - [x] task renders as a checked checkbox without a literal task marker in its label. It claimed this outcome: The exact reported two-line Markdown rendered correctly on fresh pull requests in Preview and after save/reload. The reported appearance was recreated only with different text: automatic list continuation inserted an unchecked prefix before a second full task marker, yielding - [ ] - [x] Document verification. That input correctly renders an unchecked item containing literal marker text. Review concluded: User rejected the claimed renderer failure after both Codex and Claude recommended rejection. Exact valid Markdown passes. Task-list continuation on Enter is explicitly implemented and tested; appending a second complete marker changes the input and does not establish a rendering defect. The original Mo raw body and input history were not available, so the recreated input artifact is an explanation of equivalent appearance, not a proven reconstruction of the historical run.

explanation: A feature's label does not guarantee that every optional behavior is enabled in the current installation. The reviewed example is Fuzzy search, whose ability to tolerate misspellings can be disabled by the administrator's configuration even though the search mode is available. This pattern matches a report that calls missing typo tolerance a search defect without checking that setting. A correctly enabled capability failing, or ordinary supported searches returning wrong results, requires separate evidence.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Create a pull request whose title contains a distinctive word. On the global Pull Requests page, choose Fuzzy search and search for that word with one character missing. Check the results. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that Fuzzy search tolerates a one-character typo and finds the pull request. It claimed this outcome: Fuzzy search for CrosUser showed No results with 0 Open and 0 Closed, while CrossUser found the pull request. Review concluded: Intended: typo tolerance in issue and pull request search is off by default (TYPE_BLEVE_MAX_FUZZINESS defaults to 0, documented in app.example.ini), so Fuzzy mode doesn't match misspellings unless an administrator enables it. Same reasoning as the rejected issues Fuzzy search entry; this entry is the pull requests page.

explanation: A page left open can still offer an operation that a later change has made invalid. In the reviewed case, a pull request, which proposes merging code changes, was closed elsewhere before the old page's Merge control was used. This pattern matches a demand that the merge succeed merely because the stale control remained visible, even though refusing to merge a closed request is correct. Whether the page refreshes its status after refusal is a separate question.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: Open a pull request's merge confirmation in one tab. Close the pull request in another tab. Confirm the merge in the first tab. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that confirming the merge merges the pull request. It claimed this outcome: The merge was refused with "The pull request has been closed." and the pull request stayed closed and unmerged. Review concluded: Intended: a closed pull request can't be merged, so refusing the merge with "The pull request has been closed." is correct. The page not updating to Closed afterwards is a separate accepted entry ("After a merge is refused because the pull request was closed, the page still shows it as open").
